A deterministic simulation is one whose output is fixed by its initial state and its ordered inputs, and by nothing else. In practice that means removing three things: the wall clock, ambient randomness, and any unordered iteration. Once they are gone, a run is a seed and an input log, and anyone can replay it and see exactly what you saw - which is the whole reason Atlas exists.

The short version: same seed, same inputs, same bytes out. The long version is a list of things you are no longer allowed to read - the clock, the RNG, the filesystem, the network - each replaced by a declared, ordered input. It is more discipline than cleverness, and the discipline pays for itself the first time a bug report is a file you can replay rather than a story you have to believe.

Think of it as a contract with your future self: a run you can replay is a bug you can find. Every source of variation gets named and seeded - time becomes a tick counter, randomness a seeded stream, hash-map iteration a sorted walk. Then you prove it by running twice and comparing a state hash. If the hashes differ, something read the host, and that difference is your next fix.

Rebase replays your commits on top of a different base, so the branch reads as if you had started from there. The everyday sequence is git fetch origin, git rebase origin/main, resolve any conflicts with git add and git rebase --continue, then git push --force-with-lease. Rebase local work to keep history linear; merge anything other people have already pulled, because rebasing rewrites hashes and they will have to reconcile. By family: 2xx means it worked (200 OK, 201 created, 204 nothing to return). 3xx means go elsewhere (301 permanently, 302 for now, 304 your cached copy is still good). 4xx means the request is the problem (400 malformed, 401 not signed in, 403 signed in but not allowed, 404 not here, 405 wrong method, 409 conflict, 429 slow down). 5xx means the server is the problem (500 it crashed, 502 the proxy could not reach it, 503 overloaded or in maintenance, 504 it timed out). So: 4xx, fix what you sent; 5xx, retry or page someone.

DNS turns a name into an address. Your machine asks a resolver; the resolver asks the root, then the top-level domain, then the authoritative server for that zone, caching each answer for its time-to-live. The record types you will meet: A and AAAA for addresses, CNAME for an alias, MX for mail, TXT for verification strings, NS for who is authoritative. Most "the site is down" reports that are not really down are DNS - a stale cache, a mistyped CNAME, or a TTL nobody lowered before a migration.

With customers and orders:

SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

INNER keeps only customers who have orders. LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL where there is none, which is how you find customers who have never bought: add WHERE o.id IS NULL. FULL OUTER keeps the unmatched rows from both sides. One subtlety worth knowing: a filter on the right-hand table belongs in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN, or it quietly turns back into an INNER JOIN.

patterns: how does a hash map work
replies: A hash map stores key-value pairs and finds a value by hashing the key to a bucket, so lookup, insert and delete are constant time on average. Collisions are handled by a small list per bucket or by probing the next slot, and resizing rehashes everything. The property people forget is that iteration order is an accident of the buckets: not sorted, not insertion order, and in Rust and Go deliberately different between runs. If order matters at all, sort the keys or use an ordered map - the Atlas BFS bug was exactly a hash map walked in an order nobody had promised.

It depends on what you want to keep. To drop the commit but keep the changes staged: git reset --soft HEAD~1. To keep them unstaged: git reset HEAD~1. To discard the changes too: git reset --hard HEAD~1, and be certain first. If the commit has already been pushed to a branch others use, do not rewrite it - git revert HEAD makes a new commit that undoes it. To fix only the message or add a forgotten file, git commit --amend. And whatever you reset stays in git reflog for weeks, so very little is truly lost.

The commands that cover most days: kubectl get pods -n <namespace> to see what is running (add -o wide for nodes); kubectl describe pod <name> for the events, which is where the real error usually is; kubectl logs <pod> -f, and --previous for the container that just crashed; kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh for a shell; kubectl apply -f for declaring what you want; kubectl rollout status and rollout undo for deployments; kubectl port-forward to reach a service locally. Set a default namespace once with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> and stop typing -n.

Flakiness is almost always hidden nondeterminism: unordered iteration, a real clock, a shared temp directory, a port collision, or a test that quietly depends on another having run first. Order the inputs and most of it goes away. Practically: run the failing test alone fifty times; run the suite twice with the same seed and diff; search the test path for now(), random and hash-map iteration. Quarantine what you find rather than deleting it, fix the leaked input, and bring it back.

Run the suite twice with the same seed and diff the outputs. Whatever differs is reading something you did not declare as an input - time, randomness, a directory listing, thread timing. That difference is the bug; the test is only the messenger. Bob Martinez's "Hash order bit me" is the long version of one of these, and the Stack Overflow thread on testing code that reads the clock covers the most common case.

The shape: a release has a named owner, a checklist document, a review where each section owner ticks their part, a rollback plan written before shipping, and a retro afterwards. Freeze, checklist, review, ship, watch, retro - that is the handbook's release process in six words. The checklist lives in a Google Doc everyone can tick, the review is a calendar event with the owners invited, the rollback plan is a section of the same doc, and the retro is booked before the ship so it actually happens.
